newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire prime minister resigns in face of rebel war.
newsitem.headline: Zaire prime minister resigns in face of rebel war.

text.p: Zaire's embattled Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, a victim of the rebellion in the east and political infighting in the capital, resigned on Monday, a spokesman said.
State television said ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko had accepted the resignation but asked Kengo and his government to remain in office until a successor was found.
"The prime minister handed his resignation to the President (Mobutu Sese Seko)," Zola Kinkela, spokesman for Kengo's Union of Independent Democrats (UDI), told Reuters in Kinshasa.

Under Zaire's transitional constitution, opposition parties can designate the prime minister. They were due to meet quickly and Etienne Tshisekedi, an opposition radical, was one of the leading candidates, political sources said.
The transitional parliament voted to oust Kengo and his government last week but the prime minister had earlier rejected the move as unconstitutional.
Political analysts said Kengo's decision to quit was inevitable after Mobutu effectively backed parliament's position on Monday, saying he "took note" of the anti-Kengo vote.
Kengo was appointed in 1994 as Mobutu sought a credible figure to try to restore Zaire's relations with Western donors, undermined by rampant corruption and abuse of human rights.
But he was overwhelmed, with the rest of the Kinshasa political class, by the speed and vigour of Laurent Kabila's rebellion in the east.
Only five months after launching the offensive, Kabila controls about a quarter of the vast country.
Kengo's pledges of turning the tide were empty as the indisciplined government army collapsed in the field.

Mobutu's 32-year reign is looking shakier by the day, partly because the president is struggling against prostate cancer which has kept him in Europe for most of the past eight months. He returned to Kinshasa last Friday.

A host of aspirants were jostling for the vacant premiership. On the streets of Kinshasa the most popular is Tshisekedi, a long-time Mobutu foe who has never accepted his sacking as prime minister in 1992.
"Tshisekedi has always been prime minister," one of his senior aides, Laurent Mbayo, told Reuters when asked if Tshisekedi was a candidate to succeed Kengo.
"He's been holding cabinet meetings every Thursday since 1992," Mbayo said.

The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) holds a special summit on the Zaire crisis on Wednesday in the small West African state of Togo. There was no official word from Kinshasa whether Mobutu would attend but Kabila, invited to an OAU meeting for the first time, agreed to send a delegation.

Kabila's aides told Reuters in Kisangani that Bizima Karaha, chief foreign policy strategist for the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), would attend the summit in Lome, the Togolese capital.
The aides said Kabila would not be going because of security concerns.
Togo's President Gnassingbe Eyadema, in power since 1967, is one of Mobutu's closest political friends and is among the African leaders distrusted by Zaire's rebels.
Mobutu refused to be drawn on Sunday about whether he would negotiate with Kabila. "In the next 48 hours you will know," he told reporters.
Diplomatic efforts to end the war have focused on calls for a truce and talks.
The U.N. Security Council came up with a ceasefire plan, which the Zairean government accepted, but Kabila demanded direct talks with Mobutu before a ceasefire.
U.S. and French envoys were lobbying about 20 African governments on Monday to push for a ceasefire agreement at the Lome summit, French officials said.
Belgium started airlifting paratroopers to Zaire on Monday, ready to evacuate Belgian citizens from its war-torn former colony.

Operation "Green Stream", the sixth of its kind since Zairean independence in 1960, will fly 550 Belgian soldiers to Brazzaville, the capital of Congo, which lies just across the Zaire river from the Zairean capital Kinshasa.
The United States and France have sent troops to the region, ready to rescue their citizens should that prove necessary.
